content: The Royal Australian College of General Practitioners (RACGP) is the professional organization representing general practitioners (GPs) in Australia. It is responsible for upholding standards in clinical practice, education, training, and research within Australian general practice. The RACGP has the largest membership of GPs among any medical organization in Australia, with the majority of the nation’s GPs being members. Over 22,000 GPs participate in the RACGP’s Continuing Professional Development Program. Additionally, the RACGP National Rural Faculty, with more than 5,000 members, represents the largest rural GP membership of any medical organization in the country. Historically, prior to the mid-20th century, Australian doctors typically began their careers in general practice after completing an intern year at a major teaching hospital. Some would later pursue specialist qualifications, often traveling to the UK for further training before returning to Australia. However, as the Australian population grew after World War II, the demand for specialists increased, leading to the development of local specialist training programs. This allowed doctors to enter specialist training directly after their intern year, bypassing general practice. Consequently, GPs found it increasingly difficult to retain public hospital appointments, particularly in procedural areas like surgery and obstetrics. This trend was not unique to Australia, as global medical practice shifted towards hospital-based care with advancements in pharmaceuticals and medical interventions. In the United States, the proportion of doctors identifying as GPs dropped significantly from 83% in 1931 to 18% in 1974, reflecting the rise of specialization. The fragmentation of healthcare and weakening of doctor-patient relationships due to specialization led to the establishment of professional colleges. In the US, the American Academy of General Practice (later Family Physicians) was founded in 1947. Similarly, in the UK, the introduction of the National Health Service (NHS) positioned GPs as gatekeepers of primary care, responsible for managing patient access to specialist care. Australian doctors played a significant role in defining the challenges of general practice and advocating for its professional and academic foundation. In 1950, Dr. Joseph Collings, an Australian graduate, published a critical report in The Lancet highlighting the lack of standards, academic underpinning, and evidence-based practice in general practice. His report was pivotal in establishing general practice as a specialty. The British College of General Practitioners (BCGP) was formed in 1953, with Australian doctors among its founding members, including Dr. William Connelly, the first president of the RACGP. State-based faculties of the BCGP were subsequently established across Australia. In 1957, Australian GPs declared their intention to form the Australian College of General Practitioners (ACGP), which was formally founded in 1958. State-based faculties remain integral to the RACGP’s modern-day operations. The ACGP set objectives to promote a scientific approach to disease management at the individual and family levels, prevent disease, safeguard public health, maintain high standards of general practice, support young practitioners entering the field, encourage postgraduate education, and conduct clinical research relevant to general practice. Despite these advancements, general practice in Australia faced challenges in being recognized as a medical specialty. While the RACGP is acknowledged as the specialist college for general practice, some state-based medical boards, such as those in Victoria, Queensland, and South Australia, do not consider general practice a specialty, and qualifications like the Fellowship of the RACGP (FRACGP) are not registrable. This reflects outdated perceptions of general practice as a fallback career for those who failed to pursue other specialties. Australia was one of the last developed countries to recognize general practice as a specialty, with formal recognition only occurring in 1978. In contrast, the UK and US recognized general practice as a specialty in the late 1960s. The academic and professional standing of general practice has improved significantly in recent decades, driven by the RACGP’s efforts to develop training programs, practice standards, curricula, and evidence-based guidelines. However, Australia was slow to integrate general practice into university education. The Whitlam government’s Karmel committee on medical education expansion in the 1970s introduced departments of community medicine, which delayed the recognition of general practice as a distinct academic discipline. By the mid-1970s, general practice began to gain recognition in universities, with the appointment of foundation professors in the field. However, Australia lagged behind the US and UK, which had appointed their first professors of general practice in the 1960s. Prominent figures in Australian general practice include John Murtagh, who transitioned from a rural science teacher to a leading academic in general practice. He became the first Professor of General Practice at Monash University and has held teaching positions at multiple institutions. Murtagh has made significant contributions to medical education, research, and publishing, including serving as editor of the Australian Family Physician journal and initiating the popular CHECK program for continuous clinical knowledge evaluation. His publication Practice Tips received the British Medical Association’s Best Primary Care Book Award in 2005. Murtagh was also awarded the Member of the Order of Australia for his services to medicine, particularly in education and research.
